Section 1  
What began as a routine round of Sunday politics turned, within days, into one of the strangest public arguments in recent Westminster memory. After Jeremy Hunt appeared on *The Andrew Marr Show* and declared the NHS had delivered “the biggest expansion of mental health provision in Europe”, the comment drifted across social media—until it landed in the feed of comedy actor Ralf Little. Little, accustomed to trading punchlines rather than policy, reacted bluntly: he accused the health secretary of “knowingly lying” about the figures and invited him to sue if the claim was wrong.

Section 2  
Hunt did not sue. Instead, he returned to Twitter a week later, not with a single rebuttal but with a cascade of statistics and a tone that suggested the matter could be settled by volume. He “double dared” Little to dispute the numbers, leaning on headlines, staffing totals, and training announcements to bolster the government’s narrative. The exchange carried extra charge because Hunt had recently had to retreat from a widely criticised claim to parliament about an increase of 30,000 mental health workers—an assertion later shown to be vastly inflated.

Section 3  
Little answered the challenge with stamina more than sarcasm. He posted an extended thread—more than 40 tweets—quoting reports, official datasets, and analyses from Full Fact, the independent UK fact-checking charity. The thread read less like celebrity commentary and more like a crowdsourced audit: numbers were compared, wording was scrutinised, and optimistic claims were set against uncomfortable measures such as vacancies, waiting times, and regional shortfalls. Within days it had been shared thousands of times, gathering supporters who treated it as a rare spectacle: a public figure pressing a cabinet minister not with outrage, but with citations.

Section 4  
Rather than letting the storm pass, Hunt escalated the format. On Monday he replied with a thread of his own—26 tweets—though he stumbled midstream, losing the chronology and leaving readers to piece together the sequence. Still, the message was clear: he wanted Little to defend the “lying” accusation. “Now I know you are a funny bloke,” Hunt wrote, acknowledging the actor’s trade before insisting the allegation demanded proof. He pointed to efforts to “fill the gap” in staffing, citing “8,000 MH nurses in training” and a recent announcement of an overall 25% rise in nurse training places, framing these as evidence of forward momentum.

Section 5  
As the back-and-forth rolled on, the argument widened beyond two accounts on a timeline. Hunt invoked an article from the *New York Times* to reinforce his position—only for observers to note that the piece had already been corrected multiple times after a challenge from Luciana Berger, the former shadow minister for mental health. By then, the dispute had become less about a single claim and more about trust: what counts as “expansion”, whether promises and training numbers should be treated as present reality, and how easily complex health statistics can be turned into slogans. In the end, neither side conceded, but the episode left an unusual imprint—part political spat, part public seminar on mental health provision, played out in threads, corrections, and receipts for anyone willing to scroll.
